The evaluation of antivenin reactions is complicated because serum sickness and snake bites share some signs and symptoms, and repeated snake bites can be independently associated with IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. Even in individuals who have never received previous treatment, snake antivenin can result in anaphylactoid reactions. Thrombocytopenia induced by rattlesnake venom is only partially reversed by antivenin (Crotalidae) administration, and disseminated intravascular coagulation caused by North American crotalid snakebites can occur even after antivenin treatment. The risk of severe bleeding is higher in patients who take antiplatelet drugs 60 . Tourniquets to limit systemic toxicity from the venom may lead to tissue ischemia if improperly applied. Studies have not been performed for all snakes, but tourniquet application appears to be of little benefit. DOG AND CAT BITES Key features  Bites may be unprovoked, especially with dogs  Infection is common and pathogens include Pasteurella spp. and Capnocytophaga canimorsus  Antibiotic treatment is generally considered mandatory Introduction Cat bites are commonly provoked, whereas dog bites are often unpro- voked. Dog bites are particularly common in children, and the dog is usually a family pet or a neighbor’s dog. Rabies still occurs almost everywhere in the world, with exceptions including New Zealand, parts of Europe, parts of South America, and isolated Pacific islands. Rabies associated with dog bites remains a problem in low-income countries. Fortunately, because of vaccination programs, rabies related to dog bites is rare in high-income countries, where most human rabies is associated with bat exposure. In the US, rabies is carried primarily by bats, raccoons, and skunks. Although unvaccinated dogs occasionally acquire rabies from wild animals, the canine rabies virus variant that is responsible for dog-to-dog trans- mission has not been detected in the US since 2004. Oral rabies vaccination programs using bait to target gray foxes and coyotes in Texas and raccoons in the eastern US have helped to decrease the spread of rabies. Local health authorities should be contacted to report a dog or cat bite and (if necessary) to arrange for quarantine. Latex agglutination testing of dog saliva for rabies antigen is 95% sensitive compared to fluorescent antibody testing on brain smears. A scalp biopsy from the hairy area on the nape of the neck can be sent for PCR or fluorescent antibody testing. Treatment Antivenin therapy is an important part of management and may be of benefit even when administration is delayed. Adverse reactions to antivenin include serum sickness and anaphylaxis. Preparations to treat anaphylaxis should be made before initiating antivenin therapy. Hypersensitivity to antivenin is a particular problem for those who have been previously treated. Even in individuals who have never received previous treatment, snake antivenin can result in anaphylactoid reactions. Question: Why is antivenin (Crotalidae) treatment not fully protective against all hematologic and coagulation complications of North American rattlesnake bites, and what patient population is at higher risk for severe bleeding?

Antivenin only partially reverses rattlesnake venom-induced thrombocytopenia, and disseminated intravascular coagulation caused by North American crotalid snakebites can still occur even after antivenin treatment. Patients who take antiplatelet drugs are at higher risk of severe bleeding from these bites. [Chapter: 85 Bites and Stings, p.1871]

Follicular atrophoderma can be associated with Bazex– Dupré–Christol and Conradi–Hünermann–Happle syndromes. When the lesions are found exclusively on the cheeks, the term “atropho- derma vermiculatum” applies. Atrophoderma vermiculatum can in turn be associated with various disorders discussed in the next section. Atrophoderma Vermiculatum Atrophoderma vermiculatum, a disorder limited to the face, has been described under a variety of names, including ulerythema acneiforme, acne vermoulante, atrophoderma reticulata symmetrica faciei, follicu- litis ulerythema reticulata, folliculitis ulerythemosa, and honeycomb atrophy (“ulerythema” means scar plus redness and “vermiculatum” means worm-eaten). Atrophoderma vermiculatum may: (1) occur sporadically; (2) be inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder; (3) be part of a group of related diseases that are referred to as “keratosis pilaris atrophicans” (see Table 38.2 ); or (4) be associated with various syndromes. Multiple symmetric inflammatory papules on the cheeks, presum- ably centered around hair follicles, may precede the atrophic lesions. These papules then go on to become pitted, atrophic, depressed scars in a reticulated or honeycomb pattern ( Fig. 99.8 ). The severity of erythema varies, as does the presence of milia and horny follicular plugs. Lesions can extend to the forehead and preauricular regions. Onset is usually in childhood or, less often, around puberty. Both sexes appear to be equally affected 53 , and it usually has a slowly progressive course. Atrophoderma vermiculatum can be associated with a group of closely related disorders referred to as keratosis pilaris atrophicans (see Table 38.2 ) 54 . This group also includes keratosis follicularis spinulosa decal- vans and ulerythema ophryogenes. These conditions are characterized by keratotic follicular papules, variable degrees of inflammation, and secondary atrophic scarring. Ulerythema ophryogenes (or keratosis pilaris atrophicans faciei) differs from atrophoderma vermiculatum by affecting primarily the lateral portion of the eyebrows (ophryogenes) in the form of erythema, follicular papules, and alopecia. The inheri- tance pattern is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance and occasionally autosomal recessive, with progression usually ceasing after puberty. Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans begins during childhood as keratotic follicular papules on the malar area and progresses to involve the eyebrows, scalp, and extremities, with associated scarring alopecia. In most patients, this disorder is inherited in an X-linked recessive fashion. The underlying pathogenesis in

This clinical classification is primarily of historical interest, since the two types of lesions can coexist in the same patient and their histopathology is often the same; the presence or absence of clinical inflammation at the onset of the disease is not related to prognosis 15 . Secondary anetoderma can arise in the setting of a primary inflam- matory dermatosis, skin infection or cutaneous tumor, as well as in patients with systemic disorders (e.g. autoimmune). Over the past decade, an association with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome has been highlighted. Although the vast majority of cases are sporadic, familial anetoderma has been described and is usually not associated with pre-existing lesions 16 . Clinical Features The characteristic lesions are flaccid, circumscribed areas of slack skin that are a reflection of a marked reduction or absence of dermal elastic fibers; they can appear as depressions, wrinkling, or sac-like protru- sions ( Fig. 99.3 ). These atrophic lesions vary in number from a few to hundreds, and they typically measure 1–2 cm in diameter and are skin-colored to bluish–white in color. The skin surface can be normal in appearance or wrinkled, and a central depression may be seen. Coalescence of smaller lesions can give rise to larger herniations. The examining finger sinks into a distinct pit with sharp borders as if into a hernia ring. The bulge reappears when the pressure from the finger is released. This clinical finding is referred to as the “buttonhole” sign and is similar to that observed in neurofibromas. Predilection sites for these asymptomatic lesions are the chest, back, neck, and upper extremities. Primary anetoderma usually develops in young adults, and new lesions often continue to form for many years as the older lesions fail to resolve. True secondary anetoderma implies that the characteristic atrophic lesion has appeared in the same site as a previous specific skin lesion, e.g. from varicella or leprosy. Question: How does ulerythema ophryogenes differ from atrophoderma vermiculatum in terms of the site affected and typical clinical course?

Ulerythema ophryogenes (keratosis pilaris atrophicans faciei) primarily affects the lateral eyebrows, presenting with erythema, follicular papules, and alopecia, whereas atrophoderma vermiculatum is limited to the cheeks (and can extend to the forehead/preauricular areas) with pitted, honeycomb-pattern scarring. Ulerythema ophryogenes typically stops progressing after puberty, while atrophoderma vermiculatum usually follows a slowly progressive course. [Chapter: 99 Atrophies of Connective Tissue, p.2106]

Although symptoms typically appear at least one month after drug initiation and resolve days to weeks after discon- tinuation of the responsible medication, the skin lesions of SCLE are sometimes more persistent. Tables 41.2 and 41.10 review the drugs that have been reported to induce SLE and SCLE. The pathogenesis of drug-induced SLE is not well understood, but one possibility is that reactive drug metabolites, interacting with nuclear histones, could act as haptens and activate the complement cascade. For example, procainamide-induced SLE occurs more frequently in patients who are slow acetylators as compared to rapid acetylators. While drug-induced SLE is characterized by the presence of antihistone antibodies in up to 95% of cases, these antibodies are not specific and may be seen in patients with idiopathic SLE. Antibodies against double-stranded DNA are typically absent, with the exception of TNF inhibitor-induced SLE. The seroconversion from negativity to positivity for anti-nuclear antibodies alone is not sufficient to discon- tinue a particular medication, but if symptoms develop, the culprit drug should be withdrawn. However, the anti-nuclear antibodies may persist for 6 to 12 months. In drug-induced SCLE, anti-SSA/Ro and anti-SSB/La antibodies are often present and the cutaneous and histologic findings are indistin- guishable from those seen in the idiopathic form of the disease. It therefore behooves the clinician to carefully review all medications in patients with the diagnosis of SCLE, in particular terbinafine, thiazide diuretics, proton pump inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, and taxanes (see Table 41.2 ). Of note, patients receiving TNF inhibitors may develop cutaneous lesions of chronic (discoid), subacute, or acute cutaneous LE as well as anti-nuclear and anti-DNA antibodies. Lymphomatoid drug reaction (see Ch. 121 ) Synonyms:  Pseudolymphomatous drug reaction  Drug-induced cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia A lymphomatoid drug reaction has a benign biological behavior and does not satisfy the criteria for non-Hodgkin lymphoma 57 . Although this disorder was originally thought to represent a hypersensitivity reaction, current evidence indicates that the responsible drugs may depress immunologic functions and impair immunosurveillance, leading to an abnormal clonal or non-clonal proliferation of B cells or T cells. Lymphomatoid drug reactions develop insidiously over a period of months or even years after initial administration of the culprit drug. The use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which lessen fever and other signs of infection, might delay the diagnosis and treatment of a streptococcal soft tissue infection, allowing TSS to occur 42 . Clinical features Streptococcal TSS is defined as a group A streptococcal infection with an early onset of shock and organ failure (see Table 74.8 ). The most common initial symptom is severe local pain in an extremity. Although 50% of patients display signs of a soft tissue infection (e.g. swelling, tenderness, erythema), some present with only pain and no obvious physical findings. The development of a violaceous hue, bullae, or necrosis points to a deeper infection, such as necrotizing fasciitis or myositis, and portends a worse outcome. The disease may begin insidiously with nonspecific flu-like symptoms, such as fever, chills, myalgias, and diarrhea. Symptoms of encephalopathy (e.g. confusion, altered consciousness) are commonly seen. A generalized blanching macular erythema is observed much less often than in staphy- lococcal TSS, but blistering is more likely to occur. Desquamation on the hands and feet eventually appears in 20% of patients. Shock and multi- organ failure usually develop 48–72 hours after the onset of symptoms. Complications of streptococcal TSS include renal failure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. The mortality rate for streptococcal TSS ranges from 30% to 60%. Pathology Biopsy specimens from skin lesions may show spongiosis, necrotic keratinocytes, subepidermal blister formation, and a neutrophilic and/ or lymphocytic perivascular infiltrate in the dermis 43 . Diagnosis and differential diagnosis Published criteria require isolation of group A streptococci from a sterile site for a “definite” diagnosis, combined with hypotension and clinical or laboratory abnormalities in two or more organ systems (see Table 74.8 ). Serum creatinine often rises early in the course, and creatine phospho- kinase is elevated in the setting of necrotizing fasciitis or myo­necrosis. Some advocate using antibiotics that suppress protein (and thereby toxin) synthesis, such as clindamycin or linezolid. Administration of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) may help to neutralize the toxin 34 . In severe cases of shock unresponsive to antibiotics, low-dose corticosteroids have been used 35 . Question: In streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS), what is the most common initial symptom, how does the associated skin erythema compare to that seen in staphylococcal TSS, and how soon after symptom onset do shock and multi-organ failure typically develop?

The most common initial symptom of streptococcal TSS is severe local pain in an extremity, sometimes without any obvious physical findings of soft tissue infection. A generalized blanching macular erythema, characteristic of staphylococcal TSS, occurs much less often in streptococcal TSS, although blistering is more likely to occur. Shock and multi-organ failure usually develop 48–72 hours after the onset of symptoms. [Chapter: 74 Bacterial Diseases, p.1551-1552]

~25% of skin cancers are treated with MMS in the US 10 . MMS is well suited for skin cancers at high risk for recurrence and for those tumors located in regions requiring tissue conservation and complete margin control 10 . This includes large lesions in cosmetically sensitive areas. Factors that identify a “high risk” skin cancer include clinical and histologic characteristics of the tumor, anatomic site, and history of prior treatment(s) (see Table 150.1 ). Because of the complete histologic examination of surgical margins, MMS allows tracking of unpredictable superficial or deep projections of tumor (see Fig. 150.1A ). MMS is very useful for tracking tumors that involve embryonic fusion planes, the periorbital region, nerves, and bone. It is these deep and irregular tumor extensions that are primarily responsible for the higher recurrence rates observed with other techniques. Importantly, the indications for MMS are not absolute, and any treatment decision needs to be made in collab- oration with the patient’s preferences (e.g. local vs. general anesthesia for extensive procedures), performance status, and understanding of alternative treatment options and associated cure rates. The use of MMS for the more commonly managed cutaneous malig- nancies will be reviewed first, followed by its use for unusual neoplasms ( Table 150.2 ). Basal Cell Carcinoma For primary BCCs, cure rates of 87% to 95% can be obtained with superficial ablative therapies and excision, especially on the trunk and extremities. In a meta-analysis by Rowe et al. 13 , the 5-year cure rate for primary BCC treated with MMS was 99%, as compared to 90% to 93% using standard treatments ( Table 150.3 ). For recurrent BCC treated with MMS, the 5-year cure rate was 90%–94% as compared to 80% for standard treatments (surgical excision, radiotherapy, cryotherapy, elec- trodesiccation and curettage) 14 . MMS provides superior cure rates for high-risk BCCs that are more likely to recur, including those that are large in size ( > 2 cm) or have aggressive histologic subtypes (e.g. basosquamous carcinoma 38 ) or peri- neural invasion 39,40 . Squamous Cell Carcinoma MMS offers the highest cure rates for patients with high-risk primary or recurrent SCCs. The local recurrence rates, based on a retrospective review of MMS versus non-MMS modalities for primary SCC, are out- lined in Table 150.3 16 . Question: According to this excerpt, what are the risk factors and clinical scenarios that indicate the use of MMS for treating squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)?

MMS is indicated for SCCs with risk factors for recurrence or metastasis, including tumors >2 cm, recurrent or incompletely excised tumors, tumors with ill-defined clinical margins, rapid growth, an aggressive histologic subtype, and/or perineural invasion, as well as SCCs arising in chronic scar tissue (Marjolin ulcer). It is also beneficial for immunosuppressed patients (e.g., solid organ transplant recipients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia) and those on medications like voriconazole or unopposed vemurafenib, who can develop rapidly growing SCCs. Additionally, MMS is well suited for SCCs in high-risk anatomic sites such as the lip, anogenital areas, and digits, where tissue conservation and cure rates are important. The pathognomonic sign of scabies is the burrow, which represents the tunnel excavated by a female mite as she lays eggs. Characteristic features of AD include pruritus and a chronic or chronically relapsing course, usually beginning during infancy (early onset) but occasionally first developing in adulthood (late onset) 2 . AD is a complex genetic disease and is often accompanied by other atopic disorders such as allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma, food allergies, and less often eosinophilic esophagitis. Radcliffe-Crocker called this entity granuloma annulare (GA) in 1902. Some authors consider annular elastolytic giant cell granuloma (AEGCG) to be a variant of GA; in 1975, O’Brien first referred to this entity as actinic granuloma and then it was renamed AEGCG by Hanke et al. 26 in 1979. Previous names included atypical (annular) necrobiosis lipoidica of the face and scalp 27 , Miescher’s granuloma of the face 28 , and possibly granuloma multiforme 29 . Although contro- versy continues regarding the role of actinic damage in AEGCG and whether it is simply a variant of GA 30 , in this chapter it will be considered a variant. Epidemiology Granuloma annulare typically presents during the first three to five decades of life. Subcutaneous GA occurs more commonly in children, whereas generalized GA is more often observed in older patients. While uncommon it is not a rare disease, representing 0.1%–0.4% of visits to dermatologists in several single-center studies. The female-to-male ratio is over 2 : 1, and GA is diagnosed more frequently in White patients. Compared to GA, AEGCG tends to occur in an older population. Pathogenesis The etiology of GA is unknown. Trauma, insect bite reactions, tuber- culin skin testing, vaccination, UV exposure, Borrelia , and a number of viral infections have all been proposed as inciting factors 31,32 . Based on the T cell subpopulations identified in GA lesions, a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction to an unknown antigen has been postulated as the precipitating event 33 . Morphologic similarities to other granu- lomatous processes suggest that GA is caused by a Th1 inflammatory reaction, with elevations in IL-2R-positive lymphocytes, IFN- γ - producing lymphocytes, and TNF production by macrophages 34,35 . These lymphocytes release cytokines, including macrophage inhib- itory factor, that cause monocytes to accumulate within the dermis and release lysosomal enzymes that can degrade connective tissue 36 . In addition to inflammatory gene signatures associated with Th1 and innate immunity, when lesional skin was compared to non-lesional skin, there was upregulation of Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-31) and the JAK/STAT pathway (see Fig. 128.11 ) 37 . Physical treatment modalities Ultrasound High-frequency acoustic waves are routinely used for diagnostic medical imaging, at frequencies from ~20 kHz to 10 MHz. Ultrasound is an oscillating pressure (stress) wave that propagates at the speed of sound 68,69 , with minimal scattering in soft tissues. This minimal scattering allows the ultrasound waves to be focused deeply within most soft tissues. Intensity is concentrated near the focal point, to the extent that tissue damage can occur by one or more of three mechanisms – heating, cavitation, or shock waves. Heating is favored at high ultra- sound frequencies while cavitation (a rapidly expanding gas bubble) is favored at low ultrasound frequencies; shock waves are high pressure, supersonic pressure waves that can be very destructive. Therapeutically, focused ultrasound can be used to destroy targets, such as renal calculi by shock waves, tumors by heating, and thrombi by cavitation, in addition to dermatologic applications. The attenuation (absorption) of ultrasound is greater at higher frequencies, and different materials have different attenuation coefficients 69 . Focused, pulsed ultrasound devices capable of locally destroying subcutaneous abdominal fat have been FDA-cleared for waist circum- ference reduction (see Ch. 156 ). In addition, a non-invasive, focused ultrasound device, operating at MHz frequencies, has been FDA-cleared for brow lifts. This device focuses millisecond-domain pulses at the level of the deep dermis and/or superficial fascia, up to a depth of ~4.5 mm ( Fig. 136.8 ). A small focal zone of thermal damage is produced with each pulse, sufficient to achieve tissue contraction at the focus. The treatment transducer is also used for imaging, in order to verify positioning and treatment at the proper tissue plane. This represented the first combined diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound device for dermatologic use. Cryolipolysis Cryolipolysis describes a process in which lipid-rich cells are prefer- entially affected by cold. Because lipids crystallize at temperatures well above the freezing point of tissue water, lipid-rich cells, including adipocytes and sebocytes, suffer stress and undergo apoptosis (see Ch. 156 ). Following deep cooling, cold panniculitis occurs (see Ch. 100 ) 70 , eventuating in selective loss of subcutaneous fat tissue 71,72 .

In contrast, non-thermal focused ultrasound (UltraShape Power) causes targeted cavitation of fat cells without significant heating, at a focal depth of 1.5 cm, producing minimal discomfort during treatment and rare post-procedural sequelae (mainly blistering from poor contact or treatment over bony areas), with patients able to resume activities immediately and generally having no pain, edema, or bruising. Question: In the Cre-lox system used to generate conditional knockout mice, how is tissue-specific deletion of a target gene achieved, and how can this deletion also be temporally controlled?

A transgenic mouse expressing the Cre recombinase gene linked to a tissue-specific promoter is mated with a transgenic mouse carrying the target gene flanked by two loxP sites. In progeny inheriting both constructs, Cre—a site-specific DNA recombinase—catalyzes cleavage, exchange, and ligation between the loxP sites, excising the intervening DNA only in cells where the tissue-specific promoter is active, thereby knocking out the gene selectively in that tissue. Temporal control can be added by fusing a ligand-binding domain (such as one that binds tamoxifen) to Cre recombinase, allowing the timing of gene deletion, inversion, or translocation to be regulated. Question: Why does mixed (wet) cement cause acute ulcerative skin damage, when do the necrotic changes typically appear, and which body sites are most commonly affected in chronic irritant cement dermatitis?

Wet cement causes acute ulcerative damage because of its high alkalinity, resulting from the liberation of calcium hydroxide; necrotic skin changes typically appear 8–12 hours after exposure. Chronic irritant cement dermatitis develops over months to years with continued exposure and can accompany allergic contact dermatitis to chromium. The most commonly affected sites are the lower limbs (from kneeling or contaminated footwear) and the hands (from glove contamination). [Chapter: 15 Irritant Contact Dermatitis, p.359-360]

Question: Tinea barbae typically presents in two clinical forms based on the causative organism. Describe these two forms, including the typical causative organisms and clinical features of each.

The first, more common form is caused by zoophilic dermatophytes (typically T. mentagrophytes and T. verrucosum) and tends to be severe due to the large number of terminal hair follicles in the beard area, presenting with intense inflammation, multiple follicular pustules, abscesses, sinus tracts, bacterial superinfection, kerion-like boggy plaques, constitutional symptoms, lymphadenopathy, and even scarring alopecia. The second form is superficial and less inflammatory, resembling tinea corporis, and is usually caused by T. rubrum; it may show central alopecia within the lesion, but this hair loss is reversible. Question: In the standard treatment approach for pemphigus vulgaris, what is the typical initial dose of oral prednisone, how is the therapeutic response monitored during tapering, and what is the alternative intravenous pulse therapy option for severe cases?

The typical initial dose of oral prednisone is 1 mg/kg/day, usually about 60 mg/day. Response is estimated clinically by counting new blisters per day and observing the healing rate of lesions, after which prednisone is gradually tapered; once remission is achieved, circulating autoantibody titers (via IIF or ELISA) help guide further dose adjustments. For severe cases, or if there is no response within 3–7 days, intravenous pulse therapy with 1 g/day methylprednisolone over 2–3 hours (with continuous cardiac monitoring) for 3–5 consecutive days is an alternative. Medical Therapy The TPMT pathway is important because enzyme activity varies based upon genetic polymorphisms 14 , and evaluating enzyme activity helps to guide dosing parameters. When TPMT activity within red blood cells (RBCs) is measured, which mirrors systemic activity, three subsets are identified – high, intermediate, and low activity ( Table 130.6 ). Azathioprine should be avoided in patients with low activity because of the risk of accumulating metabolites which could increase the risk of severe myelosuppression. Underdosing is possible in those with high enzyme levels and the dosage may need to be titrated upwards. Although TPMT activity may vary somewhat between different laboratories and within different batches of the same test kit, knowledge of baseline TPMT activity is clinically useful in most patients. Ethnic variations at the TPMT locus have also been described, with certain mutations unique to particular ethnic groups 14 . However, given the diversity of ethnicities, one should not profile a specific group as a means of predicting TPMT activity. Rather, the functional enzyme assay should be utilized prior to initiating azathioprine. Azathioprine dosage should be decreased by 75% in patients receiving allopurinol or febuxostat. Mechanism of Action 6-Thioguanine, the active metabolite of azathioprine, is a purine analogue similar in structure to both adenine and guanine. Instead of an amino or hydroxyl group, it contains a thiol moiety. Incorporation of 6-thioguanine into DNA and RNA inhibits purine metabolism and cell division. 6-Thioguanine has other activities which are not well understood, such as suppression of T cell function and B cell antibody production 15 . It also decreases the number of Langerhans cells in the skin and inhibits their ability to present antigens 16 . Dosages Available in 25, 50, 75, and 100 mg tablets, empiric dosing is generally started at 50 mg/day and increased to a maximum of 2.5 mg/kg/day according to clinical efficacy and careful monitoring. Question: According to the pathogenesis of irritant contact dermatitis (ICD), how does ICD differ from allergic mechanisms in terms of immune activation, and what role do keratinocytes and pattern recognition receptors play in this process?

ICD results from direct contact of a chemical or physical agent with the skin that activates the innate immune response without requiring prior sensitization, unlike allergic mechanisms. Activated keratinocytes act as signal transducers and key immunoregulators in the host's homeostatic response to these exogenous stimuli. Question: What genes and proteins are mutated in LAD-I and LAD-II, and how does each defect impair leukocyte-endothelial interactions?

LAD-I results from mutations in ITGB2, which encodes CD18, causing dysfunction of all three beta-2 integrin glycoproteins; this impairs leukocyte firm adhesion to vascular endothelium and mobilization into extravascular inflammatory sites, along with defective neutrophil and monocyte chemotaxis and phagocytosis. LAD-II is due to mutations in SLC35C1, encoding the GDP-fucose transporter-1 (FUCT1), which is needed to form sialyl-Lewis X, the fucosylated selectin ligand on leukocytes; this defect impairs the initial tethering and rolling of leukocytes on endothelial cells via interaction with E- or P-selectin. Pathogenesis A lack of blood perfusion decreases tissue resilience and leads to tissue necrosis; it also impedes wound healing by reducing the supply of oxygen, nutrients, and soluble mediators involved in the repair process. Although PAD alone infrequently precipitates ulceration, arterial insuf- ficiency plays a major role in delayed wound healing and complications including gangrene. Ischemic foot ulcers are often precipitated by trauma in a patient with relatively mild symptoms of arterial insufficiency. In such an individual, the degree of skin perfusion is sufficient to maintain cutaneous integrity but is not adequate enough to support proper wound healing. In such a setting, the ulcer will inevitably progress into a chronic wound or gangrene unless perfusion is restored 45 . Clinical Manifestations Most patients with significant PAD are symptom-free. Intermittent claudication, defined as leg pain induced by ambulation and relieved by resting, represents the earliest and the most common presenting symptom of PAD of the lower extremities. With disease progression, patients begin to complain of pain at rest, especially when the legs are elevated in bed at night, which is ameliorated by dependency. While symptoms of claudication are usually localized to the calf or the thigh, pain at rest is often felt in the feet. In advanced stages of PAD, the reduction in cutaneous blood supply may lead to ischemic ulceration and gangrene, and this may necessitate amputation 46 . Arterial ulcers are usually round with a sharply demarcated border and are characterized by an absence of bleeding ( Fig. 105.13 ). These wounds typically occur on the distal lower extremities, often over bony promi- nences. The surrounding skin may be hairless, shiny, and atrophic. VENOUS ULCERS Chronic venous disease is a common problem in adults, with its preva- lence increasing with age. Due in large part to a lack of standardized diagnostic criteria, the prevalence varies considerably, from < 1% to 17% in men and from < 1% to 40% in women 2 . Risk factors for chronic venous disease include family history, age, female sex, obesity, pregnancy, prolonged standing, and height 3 . Venous hypertension and venous insufficiency represent the most common cause of chronic leg ulcerations. Venous ulcers tend to recur, are sometimes painful, and clearly have an impact on quality of life 4 . Pathogenesis The venous system of the lower extremities consists of an intercon- nected network of superficial veins, deep veins, and perforator or communicating veins which connect the superficial and deep systems 5 (see Ch. 155 ). Throughout the superficial, communicating and deep veins, one-way bicuspid valves ensure unidirectional flow toward the deep system, thus allowing blood to flow in a cephalad direction and preventing reflux ( Fig. 105.2A ). It is primarily the contraction of calf muscles that drives blood from the leg toward the heart 4 . During standing, as leg muscles relax, venous pressure in the legs may reach up to 80 to 90 mmHg 3 . Calf muscle contractions, e.g. when walking, transiently increase pressure within the deep leg veins, propelling blood towards the heart. When pressure rises within the deep system, the valves close, preventing retrograde flow and transmission of high pressure to the superficial system 4 . HPVs do not encode the enzymes required for transcription or replication of viral DNA. Consequently, HPV is entirely dependent on the co-opting of cellular machinery for these functions. One major effect of HPV proteins E5, E6, and E7 is that the epidermal cell cycle, which is normally blocked for cells that are suprabasal, continues so that HPV genome copy number can be amplified to high levels during vegetative viral replication for assembly into virions (see Fig. 79.3 ). The E6 and E7 proteins of the high-risk mucosal HPV types act as viral oncoproteins, but no such functions are associated with the corresponding proteins of the low-risk mucosal and EV types 9 . In combination with other cellular proteins, E6 from high-risk mucosal HPV causes the ubiquitin-mediated degradation of the cellular protein p53. Elevated levels of p53 arrest cells in the G1 phase of the cell cycle or induce apoptotic cell death, so that E6-facilitated destruction of p53 removes a brake on suprabasal cell cycling. One of the principal effects of high-risk mucosal HPV E7 is to bind to the underphosphory- lated form of RB (the retinoblastoma tumor suppressor protein). A physiologic role of underphosphorylated RB is to bind to and inhibit the function of the E2F transcription factor (see Fig. 107.4 ). When HPV E7 binds RB, E2F is liberated from this inhibition and is thereby able to induce the expression of genes required for DNA replication. Both E6 and E7 are multifunctional proteins, and while their effects on p53 and RB are critical ones, additional targets are also important to the oncogenic potential of the virus. Genetic screening in familial melanoma The decision to perform genetic testing in cases of familial melanoma is multifaceted and must take into account the pretest probability of an underlying genetic basis, patient wishes, and the perceived risks, benefits, and limitations of current testing strategies. Consultation with a qualified cancer genetic counselor or specialist is recommended to fully explore these issues and provide important patient education and counseling, regardless of whether testing is actually performed. Currently, there is limited evidence as to whether genetic screening is harmful or helpful 34 . Identification of germline mutations, particularly those associated with other malignancies, may be helpful in guiding additional specialist evaluation and cancer surveillance. However, in addition to the high proportion of familial melanomas with an unknown genetic basis, testing may not identify pathogenic mutations in known susceptibility genes and variants of unknown significance may lead to greater uncertainty for both clinicians and patients. Although some have argued that knowledge of mutation status may not necessarily change dermatologic management, such as the frequency of skin exami- nations or sun protection education, studies of CDKN2A germline testing have found improved adherence to dermatologic screening and precautionary behaviors among both mutation-positive and mutation- negative patients 35 . While numerous assays for CDKN2A mutations are commercially available, they do not capture potentially relevant germline mutations in other melanoma susceptibility genes. . WOUND CLEANSERS The removal of loose debris from the wound surface is termed wound cleansing and is a component of local wound care 15 . Optimal wound cleansers should have low cytotoxicity and they include water, isotonic normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride), and in some cases, dilute acetic acid or other mild acid solutions. Isotonic normal saline is a good cleanser for the majority of wounds and a Cochrane collaboration review found clean tap water as a suitable alternative 16 . Wound cleansing can be performed via several methods: compresses (gauze squeezed so no excess fluid), soaking (saturated gauze), cleansing sprays, and high-pressure irrigation. Irrigation can cause trauma to the wound bed and is not recommended for deep wounds unless one makes sure no cleansing fluid is retained within a “pocket” in the wound. TOPICAL ANTIMICROBIALS AND DRESSINGS THAT CONTAIN ANTIMICROBIAL AGENTS The presence of bacteria in wounds may delay acute wound healing, depending upon the quantity, species, and variants of bacteria as well as their organization within the wound (e.g. biofilms). They may also contribute to delayed healing of chronic wounds, but because resident bacteria are often held in check by host resistance, most chronic wounds heal with bacteria present. That said, bacteria do compete with adjacent cells for oxygen and nutrients and they can also produce toxins that delay healing. Bacteria within wounds can also form biofilms which are complex adherent accretions that are difficult for antibiotics to penetrate. Clinically differentiating a wound in bacterial balance from a wound where bacteria are delaying healing remains a challenge. While a clean wound created with good aseptic technique (e.g. sutured surgical excision) does not require topical antimicrobials 9,10 , they may be needed for some acute and chronic wounds with critical colonization. Topical antimicrobial agents include antiseptics and antibiotics. Antiseptics non-selectively destroy or inhibit the growth of microorganisms, whereas antibiotics are only effective against specific bacteria 17 . However, there is evidence that some lesions eventuate in cutaneous melanoma. Progressive abnormalities in DNA content, cytogenetic alterations, and increased expression of melanocyte- associated antigens by immunohistochemistry have been correlated with progressive degrees of histologic atypia 60 . Although findings suggest a progression of atypical melanocytic nevi toward melanoma, atypical melanocytic nevi are not inevitable precursors to melanoma, and their presence can be viewed as a phenotypic marker of “an entire skin at risk”. Pathology Prototypic atypical melanocytic nevi are characterized by several archi- tectural features. Compared to ordinary nevi, these nevi are often larger (commonly > 5 mm in diameter), poorly circumscribed, slightly asymmetric, relatively flat (especially at the periphery of the lesion), and often show heterogeneity. In atypical melanocytic nevi, the junctional component frequently extends beyond the dermal component (the “shoulder” phenomenon). Of particular importance is architectural disorder of the intraepi- dermal component, which occurs in two patterns that are often present simultaneously to a varying degree ( Fig. 112.24 ). The first is lentig- inous melanocytic proliferation that is almost always associated with elongated epidermal rete ridges. In general, the basilar melanocytes are concentrated in the lowermost portions of the rete ridges, and the frequency of basilar melanocytes varies greatly, e.g. from one melanocyte per one to two keratinocytes to the melanocytes replacing the basilar keratinocytes and resulting in a confluent, clustered, or multilayered cellular appearance. The second pattern consists of melanocytic nests that are irregularly disposed along and between the rete ridges, as compared to ordinary nevi. These nests vary in size and shape, are often elongated, commonly have their long axes oriented along the dermal–epidermal junction, and contain variable numbers of cells. Colliding nests of melanocytes frequently fuse or “bridge”. Discohesion of cells within these nests is also common; this feature contrasts with the cohesive appearance of junctional nests of melanocytes in ordinary nevi. However, more serious chronic skin conditions, such as pyoderma gangrenosum, SLE, dermatomyositis, and vasculitis typically require longer courses with slow tapering over 6–8 or more weeks. As the dose of prednisone is decreased, the taper should be slowed. In general, a course of systemic glucocorticoids longer than 3–4 weeks can be tapered as follows, with close monitoring of disease activity: prednisone (or equivalent) > 40 mg/day – decrease by 5–10 mg weekly; 20–40 mg/day – decrease by 5 mg weekly; 10–20 mg/day – decrease by 2.5 mg weekly; and 5–10 mg/day – decrease by 1 mg every 2–3 weeks. Another method of glucocorticoid dosage tapering is to convert from daily to alternate-day therapy once the prednisone dose is about 20–30 mg/day 4 . The simplest way to convert is to multiply the previous daily dose by 2–2.5 times for the on-day dose, and taper therapy rapidly on the off-day. An alternative method is to increase the on-day dose by 5 mg increments and decrease the off-day dose by a similar amount, until therapy is eventually doubled on the on-day and stopped on the off-day. Finally, simultaneous tapering and alternate-morning conversion can be accomplished by decreasing the dose by 5 mg on the alternate morning, with the patient eventually taking the same dose every other morning as they were taking daily. Contraindications There are several contraindications to systemic or local glucocorticoid therapy 6 . Herpes simplex keratitis is considered a contraindication to local glucocorticoid treatment of the eye, whereas active tubercu- losis and systemic fungal infections are usually considered as contra- indications to systemic glucocorticoid therapy. Question: According to the tapering schedule for prednisone courses longer than 3–4 weeks, by how much should the dose be decreased weekly when the patient is taking 20–40 mg/day, and how does this differ from the tapering rate at 10–20 mg/day?

Question: A 74-year-old immobile hospitalized patient develops tense, asymptomatic bullae with clear fluid on the dorsum of the foot and ankle, surrounded by edematous skin, following an acute exacerbation of chronic lower extremity edema. What is the likely diagnosis, what underlying conditions can cause the edema leading to this, and how should it be managed?

This presentation is consistent with edema blisters, which develop during acute exacerbations of chronic edema (or anasarca) when capillary filtration rate exceeds lymphatic drainage. Underlying causes include hypoalbuminemia, congestive heart failure, renal disease, hepatic cirrhosis, venous occlusion/thrombosis, or drugs such as calcium channel blockers. Management involves treating the underlying cause of edema (e.g., diuretics, discontinuing calcium channel blockers) along with leg elevation and compressive bandages/hose, after which the blisters resolve rapidly. The association of PG with several autoinflammatory diseases points to aberrant activation of the innate immune system. Pathogenesis Because a schwannoma is a neoplastic proliferation of periaxonal or endoneurial Schwann cells, it develops as an encapsulated mass within the confines of the perineurium. Normal nerve fascicles are passively displaced to the periphery, with the bulk of the tumor appearing devoid of other normal peripheral nerve components 2 . Tight junctions not only play an important role in directly blocking passage of some molecules – they also direct epidermal differentiation and formation of the lipid barrier 4,5 . Of note, the tight junction barrier develops before the lipid barrier, both in a fetal rat model and in human epidermal equivalents (HEE), with tight junction expression receding as the lipid barrier develops 6 . The skin’s remarkable barrier properties are sustained in large part by epidermal homeostasis 1,2 , which insures that the generation of corneocytes and lipids is optimized in order to support this function 7 . The corneocytes within the stratum corneum are composed primarily of keratin filaments encased in a cornified envelope (CE), and they have been likened to “bricks”. Corneocytes are further surrounded by a cornified lipid envelope (CLE) and an extracellular milieu of lipids organized as multiple lamellar bilayers, analogous to “mortar” ( Fig. 124.1 ) 8 . At the stratum granulosum–stratum corneum interface, keratino- cytes contain abundant filament aggregating protein (filaggrin), which also plays a role in barrier function. Filaggrin has a predominance of arginine over lysine residues and is found within liquid-like kerato- hyalin condensates. As a result of their phase separation- and pH-driven assembly and disassembly during keratinocyte terminal differentiation, these membrane-less structures become osmotically active amino acids. The latter undergo deamination regulated by changes in environmental humidity 9 . As they differentiate, keratinocytes accumulate lipid-containing lamellar bodies, i.e. tubuloreticular structures, whose secreted contents play a key role in the formation of the stratum corneum (see Fig. 124.1 ). These extracellular structured lipids will comprise ~10% of the volume of the stratum corneum 10 . They prevent excessive loss of body water and likewise block entry of exogenous compounds, including most topically applied drugs (except for those that are lipid-soluble and of low molecular weight). Question: In the developmental sequence of skin barrier formation, which barrier structure (tight junctions or the lipid barrier) develops first, and what happens to tight junction expression as the lipid barrier develops? Also, in the 'brick and mortar' analogy of the stratum corneum, what structures correspond to the 'bricks' and what corresponds to the 'mortar'?

According to studies in a fetal rat model and human epidermal equivalents, the tight junction barrier develops before the lipid barrier, and tight junction expression recedes as the lipid barrier develops. In the 'brick and mortar' model of the stratum corneum, the corneocytes—composed primarily of keratin filaments encased in a cornified envelope—represent the 'bricks,' while the surrounding cornified lipid envelope and extracellular lipids organized as lamellar bilayers represent the 'mortar.' Question: What is erythema migrans, what causes it, and in what percentage of Lyme disease patients does it occur as the initial cutaneous manifestation?

Erythema migrans is an annular erythema that develops at the site of a bite from an Ixodes tick infected with Borrelia burgdorferi, and it represents the initial cutaneous manifestation of Lyme disease. It is seen in 60%–80% of patients diagnosed with Lyme disease, and multiple secondary lesions (sometimes smaller) can also occur due to spirochetemia or lymphatic spread. The lack of hair follicles, in particular replacement of the follicular bulge region by collagen and other extracellular matrix proteins, results in irreversible hair loss. Cicatricial alopecia may be primary or secondary . In primary cicatricial alopecia, the follicle is destroyed by an inflammatory process which targets the follicular unit. In secondary cicatricial alopecia, the follicle is merely an “innocent bystander” in the disease process. Examples of secondary cicatricial alopecia include deep burns, radiation dermatitis, cutaneous malignancies, cutaneous sarcoidosis, morphea, necrobiosis lipoidica, and certain chronic infections such as cutaneous tubercu- losis. The various forms of secondary cicatricial alopecia should have distinctive clinical and histologic features typical of the underlying disease. Question: What are the key clinical and etiologic features of central papillary atrophy (median rhomboid glossitis), including its location, appearance, and typical association?

Central papillary atrophy presents as a well-demarcated, diamond- or oval-shaped area of erythema and atrophy located in the midline of the dorsal tongue, anterior to the circumvallate papillae, with a surface that may be smooth or lobulated. It is consistently associated with chronic candidal infection and responds partially or completely to antifungal therapy. It may occur alone or with other sites of involvement, such as "kissing lesions" on the hard and soft palate. It affects up to 1% of adults with no sex predilection, and is seen more often in adults than children. [Chapter: 72 Oral Diseases, p.1495-1496]

In the thymus, T cells bearing the α / β TCR are subjected to a complex selection process. In contrast to antibodies, which represent the antigen receptor on B cells and recognize antigens in their naive form, the α / β TCR recognizes only short peptide fragments that are generated during antigen processing (see above). These processed antigens are presented to the TCR by MHC molecules on the cell surface. The amino acid sequences recog- nized by the TCR include those from both the MHC molecule and the antigenic peptide. Consequently, the TCR recognizes a combination of “self” MHC molecules (which are highly polymorphic) and “foreign” peptides. T cells that recognize “self” MHC molecules but not “self” peptides are useful for immune defense and do not lead to undesirable autoimmunity. This requirement is achieved by a complex process involving both positive and negative selection within the thymus. T cell development Developing T cells within the cortex of the thymus engage MHC complexes on thymic DCs. When the T cells are able to recognize these MHC molecules via their TCR, they receive a survival signal ( positive selection ). Otherwise, the T cells undergo apoptotic cell death. At this stage, more than 95% of the developing T cells die in the thymus because they are not selected due to their uselessness (i.e. inability to recognize “self” MHC molecules) 62 . In addition, T cells that express a TCR with a high affinity for the complex of a “self” peptide plus a “self” MHC molecule are eliminated by apoptosis, since they are poten- tially harmful. This process, called negative selection , takes place in the thymic medulla and involves DCs and macrophages that process and present a spectrum of “self” antigens. Question: In the thymus, what determines whether a developing T cell undergoes positive selection (survival) versus negative selection (apoptotic elimination)?

Developing T cells in the thymic cortex that can recognize self-MHC molecules via their TCR receive a survival signal (positive selection), while those unable to do so undergo apoptosis for being useless (over 95% of thymocytes die this way). Separately, in the thymic medulla, T cells whose TCR binds with high affinity to a self-peptide plus self-MHC complex are eliminated by apoptosis (negative selection) because they are potentially harmful/autoreactive, a process involving dendritic cells and macrophages presenting self-antigens. Question: What is the first-line treatment regimen for Oroya fever, and why is an adjunctive antibiotic considered necessary?

The first-line treatment for Oroya fever is chloramphenicol combined with a β-lactam antibiotic. An adjunctive agent is needed because treatment failures have been observed when chloramphenicol is used alone (as monotherapy). Without treatment, mortality from Oroya fever is approximately 40%. Question: A patient who worked in an office for 15 years with the left side of the face consistently facing a window developed nodular cutaneous elastosis with cysts and comedones (Favre–Racouchot disease) only on the exposed (left) side. Since window glass blocks UVB, what does this case indicate about the role of UVA in skin aging?

Because UVB does not penetrate window glass, yet the window-facing side of the face developed photoaging changes (nodular elastosis with cysts and comedones), this observation identifies UVA as an effective promoter of photoaging. It demonstrates that UVA alone, without UVB contribution, is sufficient to cause significant cumulative photodamage to skin. [Chapter: 86 Ultraviolet Radiation, p.1882-1883]

Question: How does the immunologic mechanism underlying photoaging differ from that underlying photocarcinogenesis, and what evidence suggests photoaging is not simply due to UV-induced inflammation?

Photocarcinogenesis is driven primarily by the immunosuppressive effects of UV light, which impair immune surveillance and allow malignant or virus-infected cells to evade removal. In contrast, photoaging results from chronic, repetitive inflammatory responses to UV light that upregulate extracellular matrix-degrading proteases and downregulate collagen synthesis, leading to collagen loss and deposition of abnormal elastotic material (actinic elastosis). However, if photoaging were purely due to this inflammation, features like wrinkling should be fully reversible with complete photoprotection, yet they are not, indicating additional mechanisms beyond simple inflammation. Activating Invasion and Metastasis Phenotypic plasticity enables cancer cell invasion, migration, and metastasis If cancers are detected early, patients can be cured by surgical excision. This is frequently achieved for cancers in the skin that are immediately visible. However, in some cases cancer cells are able to invade adjacent tissue, enter lymph and blood vessels, spread throughout the body, and colonize distant organs before they are locally resected. Histologically distinct cancer entities differ in their propensity and their patterns of metastatic dissemination. This was already noted in the late 19th century by the English surgeon Stephen Paget who proposed that the organ preference of cancer metastasis might result from favorable interactions between metastatic cancer cells and the unique tissue microenvironments in different organs. This “seed and soil” theory was complemented later to include the impact of mechanical factors such as the anatomy of vascular and lymphatic drainage from the site of a primary tumor. Research over the past several decades has provided insights into cellular and molecular mechanisms that drive cancer metastasis 50–52 . The characterization of cancer cell subpopulations that initiate and sustain the development of metastases represented a key conceptual advance. These rare metastasis-initiating cells display the stem cell-like phenotype and plasticity of their lineage progenitors that helps them to survive the adverse physical and metabolic conditions in the circulation and evade immune cell recognition and destruction 51 . Metastasis-initiating cancer cells undergo reversible epithelial-to- mesenchymal transitions and enter slow-cycling and dormant cell states during the metastatic cascade. The switch of adhesion molecules from epithelial to mesenchymal cell states, most notably from E-cadherin to N-cadherin, is regarded as a critical step in initiating migration and invasion of carcinoma cells. Inflammatory cells in the microenvironment contribute to the disassembly of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and its constituents via enzymes such as matrix metal- loproteinases (MMPs), thereby facilitating invasive growth. Dynamic adaptation of cell adhesion networks protects cancer cells from anoikis, a type of apoptosis-like destruction of cells that have lost their cell- matrix contact. Question: How does UV radiation affect the movement of melanosomes within melanocyte dendrites, and what motor proteins are responsible for anterograde versus retrograde transport?

Melanosomes move along microtubules within melanocyte dendrites using kinesin for anterograde transport and dynein for retrograde transport. UV radiation shifts this balance toward anterograde movement by increasing kinesin activity and decreasing dynein activity. Once mature melanosomes reach the cell periphery, myosin Va (linked to RAB27A via melanophilin) captures them and attaches them to the actin cytoskeleton for transfer to keratinocytes. Question: How do Waardenburg syndrome types WS1, WS2, WS3, and WS4 differ from one another in terms of dystopia canthorum and associated features?

Question: What is lupus vulgaris, what does its characteristic lesion look like on diascopy, and which body sites are most commonly affected?

Lupus vulgaris is a form of cutaneous TB occurring in previously sensitized individuals with intact cell-mediated immunity (strongly positive delayed-type hypersensitivity to tuberculin); it can arise secondarily from TB verrucosa cutis, scrofuloderma, other endogenous/exogenous sources, or after BCG inoculation. The disease has a worldwide distribution, affecting more than 200 million people in over 75 countries. Human disease can be caused by five schistosome species, most often Schistosoma haematobium , which infects the urinary system, and S. japonicum and S. mansoni , which infect the gastrointestinal tract 124 . Epidemiology Schistosomes have a two-host life cycle (see Fig. 83.24 ). Snails serve as the intermediate host, while the definitive host is species-dependent. Humans are the major definitive host for five schistosome species 124 , each of which has a specific geographic distribution ( Fig. 83.33 ): S. mansoni occurs in Africa, South America, and the Caribbean; S. japonicum in Japan, China, and the Philippines; S. haematobium in Africa and the Middle East; S. mekongi in Southeast Asia; and S. inter- calatum in West and Central Africa. The geographic distribution of schistosomiasis has changed signif- icantly in recent decades. It has been nearly eradicated from Japan and the Caribbean islands, and the transmission cycle has been interrupted in North Africa, the Philippines, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela. However, environmental changes related to water resource development and population movement have led to spread of the disease to previously non-endemic areas such as sub-Saharan Africa. Question: How can a vasovagal reaction during a local anesthetic procedure be distinguished from a true toxic or allergic reaction, and how should it be treated?

In a vasovagal reaction the patient becomes pale, sweaty, and lightheaded (possibly fainting), and although hypotension can occur, the pulse remains slow and regular, unlike a true toxic or allergic reaction. Question: According to the comparison table, how does the dermal infiltrate in lichen nitidus differ histologically from that in lichen planus, including the characteristic architectural pattern described for lichen nitidus?

Question: What demographic group is typically affected by Cronkhite–Canada syndrome, and what associated cutaneous and systemic findings accompany the lentigines in this condition?

Cronkhite–Canada syndrome typically affects older men. Lentigines appear on the buccal mucosa, face, and hands/feet, and are accompanied by diffuse non-scarring alopecia, nail dystrophy, intestinal polyposis, diarrhea, and malabsorption. Clinical parameters that aid in the differential diagnosis are the age of the patient and the location of the tumor. Myxoid liposar- comas almost always develop in individuals older than 20 years of age, and they are located in the deep soft tissue, rather than the subcutis. Nevertheless, in a child, an immature fat tumor that contains areas of marked cellularity, loss of lobulation, and mitotic figures should raise concern for a myxoid liposarcoma. Treatment Lipoblastoma, if treated with complete excision, rarely recurs. Unusual cases of spontaneous resolution without treatment exist 51 . Atypical Lipomatous Tumor/Liposarcoma Synonym:  Atypical lipoma Key features  Sarcoma of deep soft tissue that is only rarely limited to the skin  Five major histologic subtypes, ranging from locally aggressive tumors without metastatic potential to malignant neoplasms with a significant risk of metastatic dissemination  Cutaneous involvement may represent superficial extension of a deeply situated tumor  Tumors confined to the skin (“primary cutaneous liposarcoma”) usually have a good prognosis Introduction Liposarcoma is the second most common soft tissue sarcoma after malignant fibrous histiocytoma. Five histopathologic subtypes are recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO), with important prognostic, cytogenetic, molecular, and epidemiologic differences. The biologic behavior of the subtypes ranges from locally aggressive tumors without metastatic potential to highly malignant neoplasms with a significant risk of systemic spread. There is considerable controversy among soft tissue pathologists regarding the nomenclature of this tumor when it is confined to the skin. Some experts prefer the term atypical lipomatous tumor for all liposarcomas in the subcutis, because these tumors recur but have virtually no metastatic potential 53,54 . Others prefer to retain the term liposarcoma because histologically and cytogenetically these tumors are the same, regardless of location, and also because these tumors carry a small risk for dedifferentiation, which confers metastatic potential 55 . Epidemiology The annual incidence of all types of soft tissue liposarcoma is estimated at 2.5 per million, based on a Swedish study. The average age at presen- tation is 50 years. Rare cases arise in children older than 10 years of age, but virtually never in children younger than 10 years of age.

Question: In distinguishing lipoblastoma from myxoid liposarcoma, what clinical features (patient age and tumor location) favor a diagnosis of myxoid liposarcoma, and what histologic finding in a child's immature fat tumor should raise concern for this diagnosis?

Myxoid liposarcoma almost always occurs in individuals older than 20 years and arises in deep soft tissue rather than the subcutis, whereas lipoblastoma typically occurs in children. Question: In fixed drug eruptions (FDE), why can the epidermotropic migration step of the lichenoid tissue reaction be bypassed, and which T-cell populations are involved in the resulting epidermal damage at 'resting' lesion sites?

In FDE, effector CD8+ T cells responsible for epidermal damage persist as a stable population within previously affected sites even after the skin appears normal, so they do not need to newly migrate into the epidermis to cause damage. Specifically, CD8+ tissue-resident memory T cells (Trm cells) populate the epidermis of resting FDE lesions and are the principal mediators of localized tissue damage, while CD4+ and CD8+ effector memory T cells (Tem cells) recruited from the circulation also contribute. DISORDERS OF LANGERHANS CELLS AND MACROPHAGES Although cutaneous sarcoidosis most commonly presents as papules and plaques, often red–brown to violaceous in color ( Figs. 93.2A–D ), the skin manifestations are protean ( Table 93.2 ). Sarcoidal lesions are fairly symmetric in distribution and favor the nose, especially the alae, and the periocular and perioral regions of the face, followed by the neck, upper trunk, and extremities. Involvement at sites of prior injuries, e.g. scars, tattoos, is a characteristic finding ( Fig. 93.2E ). Unusual variants include hypopigmented, ichthyosiform, micropapular, psoriasiform, and ulcerative ( Fig. 93.3A,B ; see Table 93.2 ). Although many lesions are red–brown to violaceous in color, they can vary from yellow–brown to erythematous, especially in lightly pigmented skin. Upon diascopy, in which pressure induces blanching, the lesions are said to have the color of “apple jelly” ( Fig. 93.4 ); this finding is usually easier to appreciate in lightly pigmented skin. Additional variants of sarcoidosis of relevance to dermatologists include Löfgren syndrome, Darier–Roussy disease, and lupus pernio. Patients with Löfgren syndrome present acutely with fever, arthritis, hilar adenopathy, and erythema nodosum. They often require supportive measures and occasionally systemic corticosteroids, with spontaneous resolution occurring over 1–2 years. Patients with Darier– Roussy sarcoidosis present with painless, firm, subcutaneous nodules or plaques without epidermal changes. Question: Compare cryosections and formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue sections in terms of tissue architecture quality and preservation of DNA, RNA, and protein.

Cryosections, prepared from frozen samples, have lower quality tissue architecture compared to sections made from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue. However, cryosections better preserve DNA, RNA, and protein than FFPE sections. This creates a trade-off between structural preservation for morphologic analysis and molecular preservation for downstream molecular testing. [Chapter: 3 Molecular Biology, p.106]

Question: After urushiol contact, patch tests of bulla fluid are routinely negative, yet the eruption appears to spread over time. What actually explains this apparent spread, and what factors determine how quickly the eruption appears at different body sites?

The apparent spread is an illusion; bulla fluid does not propagate the eruption. Instead, differing antigen loads and variable stratum corneum thickness at different body sites cause the clinical reaction to appear at different times, so lesions seem to develop sequentially even though sensitization occurred simultaneously. A sensitized person typically develops erythematous, pruritic streaks and edematous papules that precede vesicles/bullae within 2 days (range 4–96 hours), peaking within 1–14 days, though timing varies by site. Pathogenesis Mutations are present in the gene that encodes anthrax toxin receptor 2 (ANTXR2), also referred to as capillary morphogenesis protein-2 (CMG2). ANTXR2 is a transmembrane protein that binds to laminins and types IV and VI collagen (as well as the anthrax toxin). In the skin it is thought to play a role in cell–matrix interactions and basement membrane integrity. Because ANTXR2/CMG2 is thought to target collagen VI for degradation, its dysfunction leads to an accumulation of collagen VI and a subsequent sequestration of inactive matrix metalloproteinases by excess collagen VI, thus leading to fibrosis 69 . As noted previously, mutations in ANTXR2 can lead to either mild or severe forms of HFS 70 . Missense and other in-frame mutations of the cytoplasmic domain tend to cause a phenotype with a better prognosis (JHF), whereas truncating and missense mutations of the extracel­ lular protein-binding domain lead to a more severe phenotype (ISH). Because ANTXR2 is not expressed in the brain, mental development is not impaired. Question: In hyaline fibromatosis syndrome, why do patients with ANTXR2 (CMG2) mutations retain normal mental development, and how do the location and type of mutation (cytoplasmic domain vs. extracellular protein-binding domain) determine whether the phenotype is the milder juvenile hyaline fibromatosis (JHF) or the more severe infantile systemic hyalinosis (ISH)?

Normal mental development is preserved because ANTXR2 is not expressed in the brain, so its dysfunction does not affect neural tissue. Missense and other in-frame mutations affecting the cytoplasmic domain tend to produce a milder phenotype with better prognosis (JHF), whereas truncating and missense mutations affecting the extracellular protein-binding domain lead to the more severe phenotype (ISH). Question: How do somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder differ in terms of symptom severity and patient behavior, and what treatment approach is most effective for both?

In somatic symptom disorder, patients have somatic symptoms (medically validated or unexplained) but overestimate their seriousness, leading to persistent anxious thoughts and excessive time/energy spent on them (e.g., mistaking normal hair shedding for alopecia areata). In illness anxiety disorder, somatic symptoms are absent or mild, but there is disproportionately high health-related anxiety, leading either to excessive care-seeking (e.g., daily self-exams for skin cancer) or maladaptive care-avoidance (e.g., avoiding dermatology visits despite a melanoma family history). Both disorders respond best to a combination of pharmacologic treatment (e.g., SSRIs) and non-pharmacologic measures (e.g., CBT, psychotherapy), with coordinated care among providers to avoid unnecessary evaluation and treatment.
